title: Kamsa's death

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of leaving Vrindavan: Akrura under the river, finding the boys there and in the chariot at once. What did you go back and look at again? Day nine hundred five.
screen: `LEAVING VRINDAVAN.` · `IN THE RIVER, AND IN THE CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: King Kamsa can't sleep. That afternoon, word reached the palace that a cowherd boy had walked into the festival hall and snapped the great bow on display, and fought off the guards. Now it's night, and everything Kamsa looks at seems wrong. The Bhagavata lists his omens. He looks at his reflection and can't see his head. He can't hear the sound of his own breath. He looks back for his footprints and finds none. The man who has spent the whole story hunting a child is now the one being hunted, by his own mind. Today and tomorrow, Kamsa's death.
screen: `THE GREAT BOW SNAPPED.` → `KAMSA CAN'T SLEEP.` → `NO HEAD IN THE REFLECTION.`

segments.voice: Morning comes, and with it the festival. Kamsa takes his seat on a high platform above the wrestling ground, ringed by his ministers and vassal kings. The citizens fill the stands. His champion wrestlers are ready. And at the gate, waiting for the boys, he's stationed a huge war elephant with orders to crush them. It doesn't work. Krishna fights the elephant, brings it down, and walks into the arena with one of its tusks on his shoulder, Balarama beside him. Then the Bhagavata stops the action and looks around the stands, one face at a time. To the wrestlers, Krishna looks like a thunderbolt. To the men of the city, the finest of men. To the women, love itself in a body. To the cowherds who came with him, their own kinsman. To unjust rulers, the one who will punish them. To his parents, their child. To the yogis, the highest truth. To his own clan, their deity. And to Kamsa, the text says, he looks like death. Same boy. Same moment. Same dusty arena. What each person sees depends on what each one brought in with them. The wrestlers came for a fight, and they see a weapon. His parents see their child. Kamsa brought a lifetime of fear, and fear is what walks in. Some readers take the scene as a teaching in a single picture: Krishna is met according to the heart that meets him. Tomorrow, the wrestling, and the end of the king who spent his life afraid.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT AT THE GATE.` · `A TUSK ON HIS SHOULDER.` · `ONE BOY, MANY EYES.` · then, large: `TO KAMSA, HE LOOKS LIKE DEATH.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind one person you'll see today. Notice what you're carrying toward them: an old irritation, a hope, a worry, a plan. Don't judge it. Just name what you're bringing in. Then, for a few breaths, try setting it down at the gate, and picture meeting them without it. Notice how they look then. If you pray, you can ask to meet God, or Krishna, without your armor on. The bell holds the time.
Kamsa's death. The end of the king of Mathura, who sees Krishna enter his arena and, the text says, sees death.
Your line: Kamsa's death. Today, before you walk into a room, ask yourself what you're bringing in with you. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: The story of Krishna in Mathura and Kamsa's end is recited from the Bhagavata and staged in Krishna plays and festivals in the region of Mathura and Vrindavan.

match.prompt: one boy, many eyes — tap the pairs.

myth: Kamsa sleeps soundly before the festival
he lies awake with omens: no head in his reflection, no footprints behind him.
Krishna walks into the arena carrying an elephant's tusk
he brings down the war elephant at the gate and enters with its tusk on his shoulder.
everyone in the stands sees the same thing
the Bhagavata goes face by face: a thunderbolt, a son, a kinsman, the highest truth, death.

fork.setup: you're King Kamsa. a cowherd boy has broken your great bow and your mind is full of omens. what do you do?
options: call off the festival and stay safe.
go ahead with the festival, the wrestlers and the elephant at the gate.
send for the boy to make peace.
fork.reveal: Kamsa holds the festival anyway, with his champion wrestlers ready and an elephant stationed at the gate to crush the boys.

original.note: Sanskrit: Kamsa, the king of Mathura and Krishna's uncle, whose fear drives the whole childhood story.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hero walks in and the villain is afraid.
what it means: everyone in the arena sees Krishna differently, according to what each one brought.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata pauses the fight to list each onlooker's view, and Kamsa's is death.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.42–10.43, the breaking of the bow, Kamsa's omens, the elephant at the gate, and the onlookers' differing views of Krishna in the arena

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm against Bhagavata 10.42 (the bow broken in the sacrificial arena; guards fought; Kamsa's sleepless night and omens: headless reflection, no sound of breath, no footprints — the list in the text is longer) and 10.43 (the elephant Kuvalayapida at the gate; Krishna entering with a tusk; the verse listing how each onlooker saw him).

Confirm the onlookers' list and wording against 10.43.17: wrestlers (thunderbolt), men (best of men), women (Cupid incarnate, rendered 'love itself in a body'), cowherds (kinsman), wicked rulers (chastiser), parents (child), Kamsa (death), yogis (supreme truth), Vrishnis (deity). The script omits 'the unintelligent saw the universal form'.
The line 'Krishna is met according to the heart that meets him' is the script's reading of 10.43.17; a Keeper may want to tie it to a verse or soften.
The day leaves out the episodes in Mathura before the bow (the washerman, the weaver, the garland-maker, Trivakra/Kubja); a Keeper may want one mentioned.

Editor pass: review question matches day 904's new carry; cut the stock 'does something remarkable'; cut 'the parents brought years of waiting' (not in the verse, and his birth parents were in prison); the 'met according to the heart' reading attributed to 'some readers'.
